s13.title: 694 StuyPulse | Behind the Bumpers | 2025 FRC REEFSCAPE Robot

bet.text: Score as many L4 coral as possible in auto, and design the robot around doing that fast and stably.

demand.text: L4 coral ranked first among the scoring tasks: it scores most, especially in auto, and in week 1 the team figured a robot that does L4 could probably do L1 to L3 (its shooter prototype then could not score L1 at that angle). Scoring automation and the deep climb were also must-do. Shallow climb was dropped: without a deep climb they would rather score to the last second and park.

auto.text: Four-coral routines from both halves of the reef, with paths generated on the fly, plus a one-piece plus two-algae routine the binder calls consistent. The robot can nudge partners off the starting line for the mobility ranking point.
At its first event the side auto scored three L4 coral, or two when nudging a partner; the championship's was four-piece.

cycle.text: One button aligns to the coral station; the funnel feeds the shooter and an infrared sensor sees the coral. One button per reef level raises arm and elevator, aligns to the closest branch or the side the joystick picks, and scores front or back. The arm stays up until the robot has backed clear.

endgame.text: The deep cage goes into a hole in the robot. Hooks pull it to the center and lift the robot in under half a second, and their geometry and hard stops hold it there after the robot is disabled, without a ratchet.
In one match the climb took 5 s, 4.8 s of it alignment.

fallback.text: The climb buttons double as unjam buttons: one raises the elevator to free coral, the other reverses the shooter. Software can switch off a broken mechanism or camera without affecting the other subsystems.

gave_up.text: At the championship the team called its net scoring inaccurate, and it could not take algae from the ground to the net.
The donut climb needs a hole in the belly plate and, in early tests, about a quarter of the robot's area; the bicep climb was thought to have more potential for speed.
Arm motors placed high for counterbalance raise the center of gravity.

changed.text: In week 3 the coral shooter gained algae pickup and net scoring.
The climb's planned 25:1 became 75:1, because the motor math had left out friction.
The shooter belt loosened over time and got a tensioner. Limelights overheated until each got a thermal pad, heat sink and fan.
Offseason, after the championship: the end effector was rebuilt to lift algae higher and release it more gently.

outcome.text: 47-8-0 in official play; ranked 4 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 114.11, Daly).

facts.text: WCP X2i modules, all Kraken X60
Drive reduction
Turn reduction
Frame is 29 x 29 in; the drivetrain is sized to fit the donut climb and maximize the funnel
Composite bumpers: 2.2 lb/ft^3 polyethylene foam with floor tile outside, on 18 mm birch
Bumpers mount 0.5 in above the floor, so the climb hooks can extend about 2 in past the bottom of the wheels
Bumper foam on the ground intake side was cut by 0.75 in because the intake's top rollers could not reach coral on the floor
Robot weight in late March

cost.text: Bumpers that close to the floor made the robot hard to lift by the chassis, so the team decided on eye bolts with padded carabiners to lift it

functions.name: Funnel

solves.text: Accept coral over a wide range, with no dead zones, and move it quickly to the shooter
Load from odd distances and angles while defended, since most coral comes from the human player

functions.type: wide funnel with a powered belt wall

facts.text: Belt wall of double-sided belt, driven by a Kraken X60 at
About 10 in tall and 19 in wide in the week 3 design; later versions were taller
An infrared sensor quickly detects coral entering the shooter
Planned logic: on a current spike the belt reverses for 0.5 to 1 s
Polycarbonate plates are zip tied to the elevator to limit flex
The binder also gives an unjam button that raises the elevator to free coral from dead zones in the robot
Two dead zones on the built funnel came from the coral's edge catching between belt and polycarbonate plate; removing a printed block near the exit cleared them, and later the belt was made longer
Idlers keep the belt from flexing inward
Bent 1/16 in polycarbonate plates guide coral from funnel to shooter, added because the handoff was not smooth

cost.text: At the first event coral slid and bounced straight out more than a few times

solves.text: Score L1 coral, which the coral prototypes did poorly, and collect algae from the ground

facts.text: Coral from the ground goes to L1; algae from the ground or golf tee goes to the processor
Pivot reduction, Kraken X60
Roller reduction went from 2:1, about the interview's figure, to 5:1 before the New York City event, so the rollers keep turning against a wall; the team then found them too slow for algae
2.25 in compliant wheels, 40A on the top roller and 35A on the bottom
25 in wide in the week 3 design, and a theoretical 37 in because it funnels coral at the sides; in week 7 the funneling did not work, perhaps because the top wheels were 40A and not 35A
A spline links both plates so they turn by the same angle
Mounting plates were reinforced with riveted 1/8 in angles after FEA
It waits to rise until the robot is clear of a wall or the reef
Prototype: 2 to 3 in of algae compression worked best, and about 5.5 in was tried without issue
The front roller was regeared to spin twice as fast as the bottom roller, to help funnel and score (week 7)
A new intake built before the New York City event puts the pivot chain on one side only, very close to the mounting plate so it cannot skip, with no live axle through the whole intake
That intake's pivot is 1 in lower, to score algae without it bouncing out, and nubs on the plate keep the wheels off a wall when coral is near it

cost.text: The first pivot gearing, given as 4:1, stalled the motor, and the next still drew too much current to hold the pivot up, so a 48:1 gearbox replaced it (one post says 50:1)
With a driven sprocket on each side of a dead axle, a hit on one side made the chain skip and twisted the intake
A 3/8 in hex live axle that took all the torsion bent, and became 1/2 in hex between the first two events
The first 1/8 in pocketed mounting plates bent inward; posts blame chain tension or the intake's weight
Off-season: repeated hits from more L1 scoring cracked the lexan plates and tore off bearing hats by IRI

functions.name: Shooter

solves.text: Score coral, and take reef algae to the net or processor, while being as light as possible

functions.type: belt-driven roller shooter for coral that also takes algae

facts.text: Coral roller reduction, Kraken X60
Algae wheel reduction
Double-sided belt keeps it compact
Swerve tread on the rollers tested very well for algae pickup; the offseason rebuild swapped the tread-covered wheels for 3 in compliant wheels
A beam break sees coral
Pocketed 1/4 in polycarbonate plates for shock absorption and weight
A prototype scored L2, L3 and L4 at one angle, about 40 degrees from the ground; on the robot the arm sets the angle
The week 3 plan for net scoring added no motor: plates and wheels went on an existing shaft
The prototype that led to the final one used 2.25 in wheels with a bit less than .75 in of coral compression
Rollers alone could not throw algae into the net, so the arm rotates as they release it; distance, arm start, release point and arm stop all mattered
The goal for the net shot was to make it from inside the barge zone, where the robot is protected, without the algae touching the barge pipe
By the championship net shots were angled, because head-on ones bounced out a non-negligible number of times; there are two headings, one per half of the barge
For L1 the robot aligns to a corner of the reef side so the coral turns horizontal and does not roll off; little used but pretty consistent
Off-season rebuild: much more torque at the coral rollers and algae intake, and mini ramps inside to prevent jams

cost.text: Barge shots were not accurate enough at the championship
The belt loosened over time until a small bearing tensioner was added; the offseason rebuild was rerigged to prevent belt skipping
Off-season, at Chezy Champs, the single double-sided belt that connects every shaft snapped twice in systems checks; without it the robot could only score L1 and climb

functions.name: Arm

solves.text: Angle the shooter for L2 to L4 on both sides of the robot and L1 on the front

functions.type: planetary sprocket pivot on a dead axle

facts.text: Total reduction
A 10T to 60T gear stage, then a 12T sprocket that rolls around a 60T sun sprocket
SplineXL dead axle with carbon fiber tube, fixed to the elevator plates
FEA showed most strain on the spline and one plate, so that plate became 1/4 in
Absolute encoder at 1:1
Reduction went from 16.66:1 to 20:1 with a 10T pinion in place of 12T, then to 30:1 with a 12T sprocket in place of 18T (week 7)
The whole arm weighs about 12 to 13 lb
Wires run through the axle, so the arm was planned to always turn back the way it came
Retaining rings hold the spline; in FEA the clip failed far earlier than the grooves

cost.text: Motors opposite the load sit high and raise the center of gravity
At 16.66:1 the arm wobbled severely and its characterization data fit badly; at 30:1 it moved much better within 10 minutes of retesting
The arm shifted side to side on its spline bearings, which the team blamed on the short spline tube; it packed them with shim tape, as 35 mm bearings sat on a 34.9 mm shaft
At the first event arm and shooter grew noticeably wiggly although heavily shimmed; the team suspected the bearings themselves

functions.name: Elevator

solves.text: Reach scoring height while staying as light as possible

functions.type: one-stage continuous elevator rigged inside the tubing

facts.text: One Kraken X60 with an 18 mm belt inside the tube
The binder gives a 12T pinion to a 52T gear; the interview caption reads about 50 to 14
Extension in the week 4 design
Week 4 design keeps 6 in or more of overlap between stages
Many thin riveted gussets, with 1/2 in hex shaft struts for stability
Gussets and tubes went to 1/16 in aluminum with many rivets, and the gearbox to 1/8 in, because the robot was overweight in CAD
A constant force spring holds the e-chain inside the frame perimeter

cost.text: A 1/16 in plate on it was too weak and became 1/8 in; 3/8 in hex struts bent too much and became 1/2 in
The struts' ball joints sheared more than once at the first event, which moved a Limelight slightly and affected alignment

solves.text: Hold the robot up after it is disabled without a ratchet

facts.text: Total reduction, Kraken X60
Lifts the robot in less than
Lift was designed at 5.621 in; the interview says about 5 in
Hooks are 1/4 in 7075 aluminum with edges polished to cut friction
Ground intake mounting plate and thin lexan plates funnel the cage passively
Follows a Penn State Ri3D concept
The Everybot-style cage funnel is a huge space saver and still leaves an approach as wide as the whole side of the robot (week 3)
The hooks pull a very off-center cage into the middle of the robot
First test on the complete robot lifted it in less than a second at 8 V; the lowered arm tilted it slightly, with the lowest corner still over 3 in up
FEA had points of the hooks past the yield of 6061, so they became 7075 with small fillets at the hard stops
It climbed in every match but one at the first event

cost.text: In week 1 its large footprint raised major concerns about space, especially for electronics
By design the bumper sits right at the 2.5 in limit while climbing; on the robot there was 1/8 in of leeway
At 25:1 it had too little torque for the robot's full weight, because friction was left out of the motor math; a 3:1 stage was added
Hard stops wore at the first event and the robot climbed lower until tape was added to the hooks
The chain snapped about five times when the hooks were driven slightly too far, the team's case against aluminum hard stops; polycarbonate stops worked fine for the first two events
Off-season, at IRI, an encoder offset past 360 degrees drove the hooks into the stops and broke the chain; four spare chains were used in a day
The plate that covers the chassis hole, so coral that falls in can be spun out, cracked from constant flexing

solves.text: Align accurately while up against the reef

facts.text: One camera faces the shooter side and one the funnel side
MT1 sets the gyro heading before the match, using two or more tags; MT2 takes over after it starts
Coral station, processor and barge tags are ignored because they shift over an event
Cameras are pitched to see a reef tag both against the reef and from as far away as possible
Thermal pad, heat sink and 12 V fan stopped the overheating; the radio got the same
Week 4 placement: shooter side low, pitched about 24 degrees up and turned inward; funnel side about 15 degrees and 7.8 in up, seeing a reef tag from 66.5 in to 1.7 in
Alignment chains drive-to-pose steps: a clearance pose to raise the arm, one a few centimeters off the reef to center, since bumper friction blocks centering when flush, then against the reef
Motion profiling the alignment velocity made it less jerky and kept it from ramming the reef

cost.text: The funnel-side angle that suits the reef saw the station tags only from 45 to 50 in, in week 4
Bright sun on the field upset alignment in a first-event final and caused missed L3 and net shots

solves.text: Let one driver run the robot, which leaves room for two human players

facts.text: One button per level; the robot picks the closest branch unless the joystick picks another
The robot scores front or back depending on which end faces the reef
Arm and elevator stay up until the robot has backed clear of the reef
Arm gains change with the piece held, and lowering uses gentler limits
In auto the robot skips the clearance pose and drives straight to the scoring pose, with faster arm and elevator motion
Week 5 plan for the net: the arm turns before the elevator rises, which keeps the center of gravity lower and cuts the chance of tipping
In a first-event final, when alignment was off, the driver swapped to backward scoring at L3, which was slower but more accurate
LEDs show what the robot is doing rather than which button was pressed, in case a press is not registered

cost.text: Switching reef faces during alignment could crash the robot into the reef until obstacle avoidance was added; even then it was jerky and always came close to tipping at L4 or L3

New code before the Pittsburgh event brought loop times 4x to 6x the standard 20 ms, an oscillating arm and missed shots; the team fell back to the previous event's code and never found the cause, though it suspects the pathfinding code

solves.text: Keep electronics easy to reach when the climb takes the center of the robot

facts.text: Two 1/16 in lexan plates open like a fridge door
Two CAN chains: drive and elevator on one, the other mechanisms on the second

decisions.because: in prototypes it scored L2 to L4 at one angle and tolerated almost any feed
decisions.instead_of: a roller claw, which scored slower and needed a wrist or extra pivot for L1
decisions.cost: it could not score L1 at that angle, and the final robot has an arm to angle it

decisions.because: it was simpler, climbed higher in theory (6.255 in against 2 in or more; week 4 design 5.621 in), used one motor and was less affected by the center of gravity
decisions.cost: a hole in the belly plate and a large footprint, though the team then counted it as the same space as the bicep climb

decisions.choice: Passive funnel with a belt wall
decisions.because: the belt wall cleared the jam spot
decisions.instead_of: an active funnel with horizontal rollers, which kept some dead spots
decisions.cost: running the wall toward the entry slowed feeding, so they ran it toward the shooter and planned to reverse it on a jam

decisions.choice: Net scoring from the coral shooter
decisions.because: all 18 algae fit in one alliance's net, which the team judged worth twice the processor, and it took only plates and wheels on the coral shooter; the first idea was to roll algae over the pipe
decisions.cost: it ended as a catapult motion of the arm, inaccurate at the championship, which the offseason rebuild dropped

decisions.because: it allows two human players, one at each coral station, and avoids mismatch between a driver and an operator, so the driver must have less to think about
they counterbalance the end effector, for fast rotation with minimum backlash
decisions.cost: they raise the center of gravity

decisions.choice: Hooks that lock without a ratchet
decisions.because: the hook curves lock in place without power after the climb, so no ratchet or lock pin is needed

decisions.choice: Small shooter with 2.25 in wheels, turned 90 degrees
decisions.because: the smaller wheels gave up nothing in testing, and horizontal rollers made it thinner and gave friendlier motor placement
decisions.instead_of: a shooter copied from a WCP concept, which took coral over a relatively small range of feed angles

decisions.because: nothing done in control stopped the wobble at 16.66:1, so more reduction was used to make the arm resist motion
aluminum is not forgiving when the hooks are driven slightly too far
decisions.cost: point forces dent and deform them, so they are replaced every so often

decisions.choice: Take algae off the reef right after auto
decisions.because: it clears the reef for partners and settles the driver before coral cycles

decisions.choice: Play for the coral ranking point
decisions.because: across the season, playing for it let the team score the most points
